basic_info.name: Chuong trinh GDPT 2018 (2018 General Education Curriculum / New Curriculum)
basic_info.period: 2018-present (developed 2014-2018, officially promulgated December 2018, implementation began 2020 with Grade 1, full cycle completion expected by 2025)
basic_info.key_figures: Ministry of Education and Training (MOET), Nguyen Kim Son (Minister of Education from 2021), National Assembly Standing Committee, curriculum development committees, textbook publishers (multiple approved sets), RISE Programme (research partner), World Bank, UNESCO
basic_info.legal_basis: Resolution 29-NQ/TW (November 2013, fundamental and comprehensive education reform); Resolution 88/2014/QH13 (National Assembly, on renovation of general education textbooks and curricula); Education Law 2019 (Law No. 43/2019/QH14); Circular 32/2018/TT-BGDDT (promulgating the new general education program); Various MOET circulars on textbook approval and implementation guidance

historical_context.political_backdrop: Resolution 29-NQ/TW (2013) was one of the most significant education resolutions in Vietnam's history, calling for 'fundamental and comprehensive reform' of education. The Communist Party placed education development at the top of socioeconomic development plans. The resolution emphasized strengthening political leadership alongside effective policy execution. MOET took five years (2014-2018) to develop the new curriculum. Implementation during 2020-2025 coincided with COVID-19 pandemic disruptions and political leadership transitions. Resolution 71-NQ/TW (2025) signaled further evolution, including a potential return to unified state-provided textbooks.
historical_context.economic_conditions: Vietnam achieved lower-middle-income status and was transitioning toward upper-middle-income status during the curriculum development and implementation period. GDP per capita grew from approximately $2,000 (2014) to over $4,000 (2024). The economy increasingly required workers with critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving skills rather than rote knowledge. Fourth Industrial Revolution demands drove the competency-based orientation. Manufacturing, technology, and services sectors demanded new skill sets not served by the old curriculum.
historical_context.international_influences: Vietnam's strong PISA 2012 and 2015 results demonstrated that the education system could produce globally competitive outcomes, motivating further reform rather than complacency. Global competency-based education movement (influenced by Finland, Singapore, Australia, and OECD frameworks) directly shaped the curriculum design. The RISE Programme (Research on Improving Systems of Education) provided research support. World Bank and UNESCO advisory inputs. International experience with 'one program, multiple textbooks' (Japan, South Korea models) informed the textbook policy. OECD's Education 2030 framework influenced competency definitions.
historical_context.path_dependencies: The old curriculum (pre-2018) was knowledge-based, textbook-dependent, and exam-oriented - a legacy of the Soviet model and Confucian exam tradition. Teachers were trained in and accustomed to lecture-based, teacher-centered pedagogy for decades. The single-textbook system had been in place since reunification (1975). Confucian heritage culture emphasizing authority, hierarchy, and respect for textbooks created resistance to the new student-centered approach. Assessment systems remained exam-focused, creating tension with competency-based teaching. The private tutoring ecosystem was built around the old curriculum structure.

structure_and_policy.system_design: The GDPT 2018 covers the full K-12 system (ages 6-18): Primary (Grades 1-5), Lower Secondary (Grades 6-9), Upper Secondary (Grades 10-12). Major structural features: Two phases - basic education (Grades 1-9, comprehensive development) and career orientation phase (Grades 10-12, differentiated pathways). Subjects reorganized into required subjects, elective subjects, and educational activities. New subjects introduced including Experience Activities, Informatics, and integrated subjects (Natural Science, Social Science at lower secondary). Local curriculum component (up to 20% of time) allows provincial adaptation. Cross-curricular integration of themes like STEM, financial literacy, and global citizenship.
structure_and_policy.governance: MOET sets the national curriculum framework and approves textbooks. 'One program, multiple textbooks' policy means MOET writes the curriculum standards but multiple publishers develop textbooks that are reviewed and approved by the National Council for Textbook Appraisal. Schools and districts select which approved textbook sets to use. Provincial education departments manage implementation locally. Schools have increased (though still limited) autonomy in adapting curriculum to local context through the local curriculum component. However, MOET retains centralized control over assessment frameworks, teacher standards, and quality assurance.
structure_and_policy.funding_model: Implementation funded primarily through national budget with MOET coordination. Textbook costs shifted partially to households as multiple publishers set market prices (unlike the previous single state-provided set). Government subsidies for textbooks in disadvantaged areas. Teacher retraining funded through national and provincial budgets with international support. Resolution 71 (2025) signals a return to free, state-provided unified textbooks, which would shift funding back to government. Infrastructure and equipment upgrades (labs, libraries, ICT) require significant additional investment.
structure_and_policy.curriculum_approach: Fundamental paradigm shift from knowledge-based to competency-based education. Five key qualities targeted: patriotism (yeu nuoc), compassion (nhan ai), diligence (cham chi), honesty (trung thuc), and responsibility (trach nhiem). Three general competencies: autonomy and self-learning; communication and collaboration; problem-solving and creativity. Subject-specific competencies defined for each discipline. Teaching methodology shift from teacher-centered lecture to student-centered, active learning (project-based, inquiry-based, experiential). Assessment reform: from testing factual recall to evaluating competency development. Textbooks are guides rather than prescriptive scripts - teachers expected to adapt, supplement, and select materials flexibly.

quantitative_outcomes.literacy_rates: Literacy rates remain high at approximately 96%+ nationally. The GDPT 2018 is not primarily aimed at literacy improvement (already high) but at improving quality and relevance of what is learned. Functional literacy and 21st-century literacy (digital literacy, media literacy, financial literacy) are new targets under the competency framework.
quantitative_outcomes.enrollment_stats: Primary enrollment remains near-universal (above 97%). Lower secondary net enrollment approximately 90%. Upper secondary net enrollment approximately 82.4% urban / 74.1% rural. The GDPT 2018 has not significantly changed enrollment figures (which were already high) but aims to change the quality of what enrolled students learn. The first complete cohort under the new curriculum for Grades 1-5 completed their cycle in 2024-2025. Full implementation across all 12 grades was achieved by the 2024-2025 school year.
quantitative_outcomes.international_rankings: PISA 2022 results (students partially under old curriculum) showed Vietnam scoring close to OECD average in mathematics (31st/81) and slightly below in reading (34th/81) and science (35th/81). This represented a decline from the exceptional 2012 and 2015 results. It remains to be seen whether the GDPT 2018 will improve or maintain PISA performance. Vietnam ranked 2nd in ASEAN after Singapore. Vietnam continued strong IMO performance. The 2025 SEA Primary Learning Metrics showed Vietnam ranking top in Southeast Asia for primary math, reading, and writing.
quantitative_outcomes.employment_outcomes: [uncertain] The GDPT 2018's career orientation component (Grades 10-12) aims to improve alignment between education and labor market needs. However, it is too early to assess employment outcomes for GDPT 2018 graduates as the first cohort under the new curriculum has not yet completed upper secondary education. The competency-based approach is expected to produce graduates better equipped for the labor market, but this remains an aspiration rather than a demonstrated outcome.

critique.strengths: Represents a genuine paradigm shift from knowledge transmission to competency development - the most ambitious curriculum reform in Vietnam's modern history. The 'one program, multiple textbooks' policy breaks decades of state textbook monopoly and introduces healthy competition. Student-centered pedagogy mandate aligns with global best practices. Local curriculum component (up to 20%) allows contextual adaptation. Integrated subjects (Natural Science, Social Science) promote interdisciplinary thinking. Experience Activities as a formal subject validates experiential learning. Career orientation in Grades 10-12 addresses transition to work/further study. Five qualities and three competencies provide a clear, holistic development framework.
critique.weaknesses: Implementation fidelity is the fundamental challenge: many teachers lack training, confidence, and support to teach in competency-based ways. Teacher adaptation is hindered by unclear guidance, heavier workloads, and insufficient professional development. Multiple textbook sets create confusion for teachers and parents, and inconsistencies between curriculum, textbooks, and assessment methods emerge. Assessment reform lags behind curriculum reform - exams still largely test factual recall. Class sizes remain too large for student-centered methods (40-50 students per class in many schools). Resource constraints: many schools lack labs, libraries, ICT equipment, and learning materials needed for the new approach. Urban-rural implementation gap: rural and remote schools are least prepared for the transition.
critique.controversies: The 'one program, multiple textbooks' policy became highly controversial: some educators and politicians argued for returning to a single unified textbook set. By 2025, Resolution 71 signaled a move back toward unified state textbooks, effectively reversing a key GDPT 2018 policy after just 5 years. Inconsistencies between approved textbook sets raised quality concerns. Some textbook content was publicly criticized for errors or inappropriate material. The pace of implementation was debated: critics said it was too rushed; supporters argued faster reform was needed. The balance between national standards and local adaptation proved contentious. Teacher workload increases without corresponding compensation increases generated widespread frustration.
critique.unintended_consequences: Teachers feeling overwhelmed by new requirements without adequate support has led to superficial compliance rather than genuine pedagogical transformation. Many teachers were unaware of the additional teaching options provided by the new curriculum. The multiple textbook market created a commercial textbook industry with profit incentives that sometimes conflicted with educational quality. Increased teacher autonomy was experienced as burden rather than empowerment due to lack of preparation. Assessment systems that remain exam-focused undermine the competency-based curriculum - teachers teach to the test rather than to competency development. The tutoring market adapted to the new curriculum rather than diminishing. Implementation created additional financial burdens on families purchasing new textbooks.

equity_and_inequality.urban_rural_gap: The implementation gap between urban and rural schools is a primary concern. Urban schools have better-trained teachers, more resources, and greater capacity to implement competency-based teaching. Rural schools face shortages of equipment, materials, and qualified teachers for new subjects (e.g., Informatics, integrated sciences). The multiple textbook policy may disadvantage rural areas where teachers have less capacity to select and adapt materials. The local curriculum component could either reduce the gap (by allowing relevant local content) or widen it (if rural schools lack capacity to develop quality local curriculum).
equity_and_inequality.ethnic_minority_access: Ethnic minority students face compounded disadvantages in the GDPT 2018 implementation. Language barriers are exacerbated when the curriculum demands higher-order thinking and expression skills in Vietnamese. Teachers in ethnic minority areas are often least prepared for the competency-based shift. The local curriculum component could benefit ethnic minority areas by incorporating indigenous knowledge and languages, but implementation capacity is limited. Dropout rates for non-Kinh students remain approximately double those of Kinh students. Access to supplementary resources and tutoring to support the new curriculum is much lower in ethnic minority communities.
equity_and_inequality.gender_disparities: The GDPT 2018 does not explicitly address gender disparities but the competency-based approach may benefit girls by valuing collaboration, communication, and creative skills alongside traditional academic metrics. Gender parity at primary and lower secondary levels is relatively good. However, STEM subject tracking at upper secondary may perpetuate gender patterns. Girls from ethnic minority communities face particular challenges. Career orientation in Grades 10-12 could either reinforce or challenge gendered career assumptions depending on implementation.
equity_and_inequality.disability_inclusion: The GDPT 2018 aligns with the 2019 Education Law's mandate for inclusive education as the preferred mode. The curriculum is designed to be adaptable to different learning needs. However, practical inclusion remains limited: most teachers lack training in differentiated instruction; classroom resources for students with disabilities are scarce; physical accessibility of schools is often poor; assessment accommodations are inconsistent. The competency-based framework theoretically supports individualized progress, but class sizes and teacher capacity prevent this in practice.
equity_and_inequality.socioeconomic_stratification: The GDPT 2018 may inadvertently deepen stratification. Wealthy families can access better tutoring aligned with the new curriculum, better textbooks, and supplementary materials. International schools have greater capacity to implement competency-based education effectively. The textbook market creates cost differentials. Public schools in wealthy districts implement the reform more effectively than those in poor areas. The shadow education system adapts faster to curriculum changes in urban areas, maintaining the advantage for families who can afford supplementary education.

comparative.vs_asean_peers: Vietnam's GDPT 2018 is among the most ambitious curriculum reforms in ASEAN. Thailand's 2008 Basic Education Core Curriculum also shifted toward competency-based education but with mixed implementation results. Indonesia's 2013 Kurikulum and subsequent Merdeka Belajar share similar competency-based goals. Philippines' K-12 reform (2013) was more structural (adding 2 years). Singapore's 'Teach Less, Learn More' initiative is a comparable philosophical shift. Vietnam's implementation challenges mirror those experienced by ASEAN peers: teacher capacity gaps, assessment lag, and urban-rural disparities.
comparative.vs_aspirational_models: Finland's competency-based national curriculum (2016 revision) is an aspirational model but Finland has smaller class sizes, better-compensated teachers, and no standardized testing. Singapore's framework emphasizes 21st-century competencies with better resources and teacher development. South Korea's curriculum reforms face similar challenges of exam culture undermining competency goals. Japan's 'one program, multiple textbooks' system provided a direct model for Vietnam's policy. Australia's Australian Curriculum was another reference point for competency frameworks. Vietnam's resource constraints and teacher readiness gap mean implementation will take longer than in these reference countries.
comparative.unesco_framework: ISCED mapping: Primary (ISCED 1, Grades 1-5), Lower Secondary (ISCED 2, Grades 6-9), Upper Secondary (ISCED 3, Grades 10-12). The GDPT 2018's competency-based orientation aligns with UNESCO's emphasis on learning outcomes (SDG 4). The career orientation phase aligns with ISCED's distinction between general and vocational upper secondary pathways. The curriculum's five qualities and three competencies map to UNESCO's four pillars of learning and OECD's Education 2030 Learning Compass.

ideological_framework.communist_party_goals: Resolution 29 (2013) established that the GDPT 2018 should serve both national development and socialist ideological goals. The five key qualities include 'patriotism' (yeu nuoc) as the first quality, reflecting Party priorities. Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought remain in the curriculum through Citizenship Education and related subjects. The Party called for 'stronger involvement of the Communist Party in the education system' alongside reform. The tension between cultivating critical thinking (a competency goal) and maintaining ideological conformity (a Party goal) is a fundamental unresolved tension in the reform.
ideological_framework.confucian_legacy: The GDPT 2018 directly challenges some Confucian educational norms: student-centered learning challenges teacher authority; multiple textbooks challenge the sanctity of the single text; competency over knowledge challenges the exam-focused tradition. However, Confucian values persist: respect for education, teacher reverence, and family investment drive implementation effort. The five qualities framework echoes Confucian virtues. Vietnamese teachers' 'career adaptability in implementing the 2018 competency-oriented curriculum' is studied specifically 'within a Confucian heritage culture,' acknowledging this tension. The exam culture remains the single biggest cultural barrier to competency-based implementation.
ideological_framework.modernization_ideology: The GDPT 2018 is explicitly framed as preparing Vietnam for the Fourth Industrial Revolution and knowledge economy. The curriculum embodies the modernization ideal of developing human capital for national competitiveness. Digital literacy, coding, and STEM integration reflect this orientation. The spirit of 'Khai dan tri' (enlighten the people) is modernized through competency development and critical thinking goals. The career orientation component links education directly to economic participation. The reform represents the latest iteration of Vietnam's century-long project of educational modernization.

reform_trajectory.past_reforms: Resolution 29 (2013) was the catalyst for the GDPT 2018, itself building on decades of incremental reform attempts. The 2005 Education Law's quality improvement goals were largely unmet. Previous curriculum revisions (2000, 2006) made changes within the knowledge-based paradigm rather than transforming it. Key lesson learned: curriculum documents alone do not change classroom practice - teacher development and assessment reform must accompany curriculum change. The failure of previous surface-level reforms motivated the more fundamental approach of GDPT 2018.
reform_trajectory.current_initiatives: Active implementation initiatives: phased grade-by-grade rollout (completed Grade 1-12 by 2024-2025); massive teacher retraining programs (workshops, online courses, peer learning); textbook development and approval by multiple publishers; assessment framework revision (ongoing but slow); school infrastructure upgrades; digital platform development for curriculum resources; local curriculum development in provinces; integration of STEM education; Experience Activities implementation; school-based curriculum adaptation training.
reform_trajectory.future_vision: Resolution 71 (2025) sets the next phase: by 2030, 80% of schools to meet national education standards; unified state-provided textbooks (reversing the multiple textbook policy); stronger STEM and AI literacy integration; digital transformation in teaching and assessment; reduced reliance on private tutoring. By 2045: Vietnam's education system among the world's top 20. The GDPT 2018 framework is expected to evolve rather than be replaced, with adjustments based on implementation experience and Resolution 71's direction. Assessment reform remains the critical next frontier.
reform_trajectory.implementation_fidelity: Implementation fidelity is the defining challenge. Research documents significant gaps: teachers still control content and pace of learning despite student-centered mandates; teachers continue to rely on extrinsic rather than intrinsic motivation; limited opportunities for genuine student reflection and deeper understanding; many teachers unaware of curriculum flexibility options; technology education undermined by resource constraints; big class sizes (40-50 students) prevent student-centered methods; mixed-level classes challenge differentiated instruction; heavy teacher workloads limit preparation time; the gap between ambitious policy goals and classroom reality remains Vietnam's most persistent education challenge.

human_dimension.teacher_experience: Teachers are at the center of the GDPT 2018's success or failure, and many are struggling. Challenges include: actively studying and developing new professional skills; flexibly selecting and using appropriate textbooks; adjusting teaching to meet student diversity; heavier workloads without proportionate compensation increases. Many find increased autonomy challenging due to unclear guidance and insufficient support. Teacher training programs have reached large numbers but depth and quality vary. Salary remains inadequate (mean approximately 10 million VND/month), driving continued moonlighting. Teacher agency is constrained by institutional culture, assessment pressures, and resource limitations. Younger teachers tend to adapt more readily than experienced teachers trained entirely in the old paradigm.
human_dimension.student_experience: Students in the GDPT 2018 are expected to experience more active, engaging, and relevant learning. In practice, experience varies enormously by school quality and location. In well-resourced urban schools, students may experience project-based learning, group work, and creative activities. In under-resourced schools, the experience may differ little from the old curriculum. Students still face heavy academic pressure, extensive homework, and private tutoring expectations. The first primary cohort (entering Grade 1 in 2020) has completed the new curriculum cycle and should show measurable differences. Mental health support remains largely absent despite reform rhetoric.
human_dimension.parent_perspective: Parents have been confused and sometimes frustrated by the GDPT 2018 changes. Multiple textbook sets created uncertainty about which materials to buy. Changes in teaching methods left parents unable to help with homework as they would have in the past. Some parents perceive the competency-based approach as less rigorous than the old knowledge-focused curriculum. Parental spending on education has not decreased as the tutoring market adapted to the new curriculum. Parents remain focused on examination outcomes regardless of curriculum philosophy changes. The potential return to unified textbooks (Resolution 71) was welcomed by many parents.
human_dimension.cultural_attitudes: The GDPT 2018 challenges deeply held cultural attitudes about education. The shift from knowledge authority (teacher as sole expert) to facilitated learning challenges the Confucian teacher-student hierarchy. Multiple textbooks challenge the cultural reverence for a single authoritative text. Competency-based assessment challenges the exam-result-focused culture. However, the cultural value placed on education drives engagement with reform - families invest heavily in understanding and supporting the new curriculum. Teachers Day celebrations and respect for the teaching profession persist. The tension between innovation and tradition defines the cultural reception of the reform.

economic_dimensions.public_spending: Education spending is approximately 2.89% of GDP (2022), down from a peak of 5.65% (2013 - the year Resolution 29 was passed). As a share of the national budget, education receives approximately 15-20%. Resolution 71 (2025) commits to maintaining at least 20% of the state budget for education. GDPT 2018 implementation requires significant additional spending on teacher training, textbook development, infrastructure, and equipment. The gap between implementation ambitions and available funding constrains reform effectiveness.
economic_dimensions.household_spending: Household spending on education remains high and may have increased with the GDPT 2018 changes. New textbooks from multiple publishers cost more than the previous single state-provided set. Tutoring adapted to the new curriculum continues as a major household expense. Vietnam averages approximately 6 hours of tutoring per week - an extreme global outlier. Equipment and material costs for new subjects (STEM, Informatics, Experience Activities) add expenses. The 2019 Law provides some tuition exemptions but does not cover the full household education cost burden.
economic_dimensions.teacher_compensation: Teacher compensation remains inadequate relative to the demands of the GDPT 2018. Mean salary approximately 10.153 million VND/month. The reform demands more preparation time, professional development, and creativity from teachers without proportionate salary increases. Over 60% of teachers engage in supplementary employment. Resolution 71 (2025) mandates a minimum 70% teaching allowance. The gap between compensation and expectations is a primary barrier to reform implementation. Teachers who are most engaged with the new curriculum may actually earn less (spending more time on preparation) unless they can monetize their expertise through tutoring.
economic_dimensions.edtech_market: The EdTech market has grown partly in response to GDPT 2018 needs. Market valued at approximately USD 1.0 billion in 2024. Approximately 750 EdTech companies operate in Vietnam, with 80% targeting K-12. COVID-19 accelerated adoption. Key investments include Kyna English ($16M total), Vuihoc.vn ($6M), TEKY ($5M). Digital platforms for curriculum resources, online tutoring, and learning management are expanding. EdTech could support GDPT 2018 implementation through scalable teacher training, digital learning resources, and competency-based assessment tools. However, digital divide between urban and rural schools limits EdTech impact.

shadow_education.tutoring_market: The private tutoring market has adapted to rather than diminished under the GDPT 2018. Vietnam's approximately 6 hours/week of tutoring is three times the expected global trend. Teachers continue to supplement inadequate salaries through tutoring. The new curriculum's complexity may have increased demand for tutoring as parents feel less able to support children's learning themselves. Tutoring in competency-based skills (presentations, projects, creative work) has emerged alongside traditional subject tutoring. Resolution 71 (2025) explicitly calls for 'comprehensive measures to reduce excessive reliance on private tutoring,' acknowledging the problem persists. The fundamental driver (low teacher salaries) remains unresolved.
shadow_education.test_prep_industry: [uncertain] Test preparation remains significant as long as high-stakes examinations persist. The national high school graduation exam and university entrance process continue to drive test prep demand. Commercial tutoring centers and online platforms offer exam preparation courses. The GDPT 2018's competency-based assessment goals have not yet significantly changed the test preparation market because assessment reform lags behind curriculum reform. International test preparation (IELTS, TOEFL, SAT) has grown as overseas education aspirations increase.
shadow_education.international_school_tier: International schools represent an alternative to the GDPT 2018 curriculum. Vietnam has 21 IB World Schools. International schools offering IB, Cambridge, AP, and other curricula serve wealthy urban families seeking alternatives to public education. These schools generally implement competency-based approaches more effectively due to smaller class sizes, better resources, and teacher training. Annual fees range from $5,000 to $30,000+. The international school tier highlights the stratification that the GDPT 2018 aims to address but may inadvertently reinforce: families with means opt out of the public system entirely.
